title: Make a Bulb Light Up
subtitle: What a bulb really needs, and why two bulbs in a row shine dimmer than one.

sections.title: What does a bulb need?
sections.body:
Take a battery, a bulb and a piece of wire. Can you make the bulb glow? Most people try touching one end of the bulb to one end of the battery, and nothing happens. That is not bad luck. It is the first big idea in electricity.

A bulb only glows when electricity can travel all the way around and come back to where it started. That path is called a circuit, which is just a Latin-sounding word for "circle". A circuit with a gap in it is called an open circuit, and an unbroken one is a closed circuit.

In this lesson you will build the circuit, open and close it, and then put in a second bulb to see what changes. Every picture on the page is a real, running experiment. Press Simulate on each one.

sections.title: Your first closed circuit
sections.body:
Here is a battery, a switch, a bulb and a meter called an ammeter. The ammeter counts how much electricity is flowing past it each second. That flow is called current, and we measure it in amperes (A) or in thousandths of an ampere, milliamperes (mA).

The switch is closed, so the loop is complete. Press Simulate and look at two things: the bulb, and the number on the ammeter.

figures.caption: Figure 1.1 — a battery, a closed switch, a bulb and an ammeter
figures.note: Press Simulate. The bulb glows and the ammeter shows about 500 mA.

sections.title: What if the switch is open?
sections.body: Scientists make a guess before they look. Guess now, and then the experiment will show you who was right.

questions.prompt: You open the switch, so there is a gap in the circuit. What happens to the bulb?

choices.text: It glows, but a little dimmer, because some electricity still leaks through.
It glows brighter, because the electricity is waiting at the gap.

responses.title: Nice thought, but there is no leak.
responses.body: A gap in a wire does not let a little electricity through. Air is an excellent insulator, so across a small gap the current is not "small", it is zero. The bulb is either in a complete loop or it is not.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: With a gap, nothing can flow around the loop, so the current is zero and the bulb is dark. This is exactly how a light switch on your wall works: it opens or closes a gap in the circuit.

responses.title: Electricity does not queue up.
responses.body: Charges only move when there is a complete path. A gap does not store the flow to release later. If one part of the loop cannot pass current, no part of the loop can, so the bulb gets nothing.

verify.caption: Check it — the same circuit with the switch open
verify.note: Press Simulate: the ammeter reads 0 and the bulb stays dark.

sections.title: Electricity is like water in a pipe
sections.body:
It helps to picture a loop of pipe full of water, with a pump in it. The battery is the pump: it pushes. The wire is the pipe. The bulb is a narrow, rough section of pipe that is hard to push water through.

The push is called voltage (measured in volts, V). How hard the bulb makes it to flow is called resistance (measured in ohms, Ω). How much water flows past each second is the current. A stronger pump gives more flow. A narrower, rougher pipe gives less.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2 — the pipe picture next to the real circuit words
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
[Battery = the pump] as p #blue
[Wire = the pipe] as w #mint
[Bulb = a narrow pipe] as b #amber
[Current = water flowing each second] as c #violet
p -> w : pushes
w -> b
b -> c : sets how much
c -> p : comes back");

sections.title: Two bulbs in a row
sections.body:
Now put a second bulb in the same loop, right after the first. Electricity has one road only, and it must squeeze through both bulbs one after the other. This is called a series circuit.

Each bulb is the same, 12 Ω. Two of them in a row are harder to push current through than one, so the total resistance is 12 + 12 = 24 Ω.

figures.caption: Figure 1.3 — two bulbs in series
figures.note: Press Simulate: the current is only 250 mA, half of Figure 1.1, so both bulbs shine dimmer.

questions.prompt: In a series circuit, one of the two bulbs is unscrewed and removed. What happens to the other bulb?

choices.text: It stays lit, because it still has the battery.
It goes dark, because the loop now has a gap.

responses.title: The battery is not the only thing it needs.
responses.body: A bulb needs a complete loop, not just a battery. In a series circuit there is only one road, and the missing bulb leaves a gap in it, so no current flows to either bulb.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: In series there is only one path. Remove one bulb and you have opened the circuit, so every bulb goes dark. Old Christmas lights wired this way were famous for it: one dead bulb and the whole string went out.

responses.title: It would be nice, but no.
responses.body: Nothing speeds up when a bulb is removed. The current falls to zero, because the loop is broken, so the remaining bulb gets no current at all.

sections.title: Two bulbs side by side
sections.body:
There is another way to add the second bulb: give each bulb its own road straight to the battery. This is a parallel circuit. Each bulb gets the full push of the battery, so each shines as brightly as it would alone.

The battery now has two roads to send current down, so the total current doubles: 500 mA for each bulb makes 1000 mA, which is 1 A. This is how the lights in your house are wired. Switch one off and the others stay on.

figures.caption: Figure 1.4 — two bulbs in parallel
figures.note: Press Simulate: the ammeter at the battery reads about 1 A (999.8 mA), twice Figure 1.1.

sections.title: Working out the current
sections.body: There is a rule that links the three ideas, and it is the most useful one in the whole chapter: current = voltage ÷ resistance. In letters, I = V ÷ R. This rule is called Ohm's law.

worked.why: Write down what you know. The battery is 6 V and the bulb is 12 Ω.
Pick the rule that links them. We want current, so divide voltage by resistance.
Put the numbers in and do the division.

Check your answer against the experiment. 0.5 A is the same as 500 mA, which is what the ammeter in Figure 1.1 showed (it reads 499.9 mA, a hair under, because real wires and batteries have a tiny resistance too).

problems.prompt: A 9 V battery is connected to a 18 Ω bulb. How much current flows?
problems.answer: Divide voltage by resistance: 9 ÷ 18 = 0.5 A, which is 500 mA.

problems.prompt: Two 12 Ω bulbs are in series with a 6 V battery. What is the total resistance, and what current flows?
problems.answer: In series the resistances add: 12 + 12 = 24 Ω. Then 6 ÷ 24 = 0.25 A, or 250 mA, which is what Figure 1.3 shows.

verify.caption: Check it — two bulbs in series

problems.prompt: In your home, why are the lights wired in parallel and not in series?
problems.answer: In parallel each light gets the full voltage and works on its own, so one bulb failing or being switched off does not turn the others off. In series they would all depend on each other and all be dimmer.
